author_or_institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: 2025 AI Index Report — Research and Development
book_use: Chapter 1: fixed-performance inference cost fell from roughly $20 per million tokens in November 2022 to $0.07 in October 2024 at the GPT-3.5-equivalent MMLU threshold; use as a historical comparison, not as a claim that tokens equal thoughts.

author_or_institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: 2026 AI Index Report — Economy
book_use: Chapter 1: context for organizational adoption and estimates of rising U.S. consumer surplus from generative AI while many tools remain free or close to it; consumer surplus is not provider revenue or investor return.

author_or_institution: METR
title: Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models
book_use: Chapter 1: describes longer agentic software tasks probabilistically against human-expert completion time; do not generalize directly to all occupations or real-world autonomy.

author_or_institution: Erik Brynjolfsson; Danielle Li; Lindsey R. Raymond
title: Generative AI at Work
book_use: Chapter 1: setting-specific causal evidence from customer support, including roughly 14% average productivity improvement and larger gains for novice or lower-skilled workers.

author_or_institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: 2026 AI Index Report — Research and Development
book_use: Chapter 2: context on rapid AI compute-capacity growth, data-center buildout, hardware concentration, and environmental or resource constraints; supports coexistence of upstream scarcity with cheap downstream inference.

author_or_institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: 2026 AI Index Report — Technical Performance
book_use: Chapter 2: evidence of rapid benchmark gains alongside jagged capabilities and persistent failures on apparently simpler tasks; benchmark performance is not deployment reliability.

author_or_institution: Julie Holland Mortimer; Chris Nosko; Alan Sorensen
title: Supply Responses to Digital Distribution: Recorded Music and Live Performances
book_use: Chapter 3: file sharing reduced album sales while increasing live-performance revenue for smaller artists, with negligible live-revenue effects for large established artists. Supports conditional complement migration rather than a universal claim that live revenue replaces recorded revenue.

author_or_institution: Federal Communications Commission
title: The Information Needs of Communities
source_type: Federal policy report using Newspaper Association of America data
book_use: Chapter 3: U.S. newspaper classified-ad revenue fell from about $19.6B in 2000 to $5.6B in 2010 as recession effects combined with migration toward Craigslist and specialized online marketplaces. Use to show unbundling and lost cross-subsidy, not to attribute the full decline to one platform or technology.

author_or_institution: Anthropic
title: Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise
book_use: Chapter 4: analysis of roughly 400,000 Claude Code sessions in which humans make more planning decisions while Claude makes more execution decisions and expertise remains associated with better outcomes; platform-specific evidence.

author_or_institution: Anthropic
title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Learning curves
book_use: Chapter 4: more experienced Claude users attempt higher-value tasks and are more likely to elicit successful responses; Claude usage is not representative of the whole labor market.

author_or_institution: Anthropic
title: Anthropic Economic Index report: Cadences
book_use: Chapter 4: updated evidence on longer-running agentic tasks and automation versus augmentation modes; methodology and product mix continue to change.

author_or_institution: Hamsa Bastani; Osbert Bastani; Alp Sungu; Haosen Ge; Özge Kabakcı; Rei Mariman
title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
book_use: Chapter 4: nearly 1,000 students; standard GPT-4 access improved assisted practice performance but reduced later unassisted exam performance by 17%, while a teacher-informed guarded tutor largely eliminated that learning penalty. Use as a bounded mechanism for skill acquisition, not a general claim about workplace deskilling.

author_or_institution: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua et al.
title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
book_use: Chapters 9 and 12: 758 BCG consultants; AI improved speed and quality on tasks inside the tested capability frontier but harmed performance on an outside-frontier task. Supports heterogeneous gains and judgment risk, not universal professional replacement.

author_or_institution: Eleanor W. Dillon; Sonia Jaffe; Nicole Immorlica; Christopher T. Stanton
title: Shifting Work Patterns with Generative AI
source_type: NBER working paper and randomized field experiment
book_use: Chapters 9 and 12: 66 firms and 7,137 knowledge workers; adopters saved roughly two email hours weekly but individual AI access did not produce broad detected changes in task quantity or composition. Supports coordination as a persistent bottleneck.

author_or_institution: Zheyuan Cui; Mert Demirer; Sonia Jaffe; Leon Musolff; Sida Peng; Tobias Salz
title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
book_use: Chapter 10: pooled experiments across 4,867 developers found 26.08% more completed tasks with an AI coding assistant, with higher adoption and larger gains among less experienced developers; setting-specific evidence, not an economy-wide replacement estimate.

author_or_institution: Erik Brynjolfsson; Danielle Li; Lindsey R. Raymond
title: Generative AI at Work
book_use: Chapter 10: 5,172 customer-support agents; average productivity rose about 15%, with larger gains among less experienced workers and small quality declines among the most experienced. Supports compression of some output differences while preserving heterogeneity.

author_or_institution: American Bar Association Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
title: Formal Opinion 512: Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools
book_use: Chapter 11: lawyers may use generative AI but existing duties of competence, confidentiality, communication, supervision, candor, and reasonable fees remain. Use as an institutional example of production scaling without responsibility disappearing.

author_or_institution: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence
title: 2026 AI Index Report — Responsible AI
book_use: Chapter 12: documents continuing calibration and hallucination problems across leading models and strong sensitivity to benchmark framing; do not translate benchmark hallucination rates into ordinary-use error rates.

author_or_institution: Philipp Lorenz-Spreen; Bjarke Mørch Mønsted; Philipp Hövel; Sune Lehmann
title: Accelerating dynamics of collective attention
book_use: Chapter 13: attention cycles shortened across several cultural domains, with increasing content production and consumption rates implicated in the model; evidence concerns collective attention dynamics, not a universal fall in individual biological attention span.

author_or_institution: Luca Bellaiche et al.
title: Understanding how personality traits, experiences, and attitudes shape negative bias toward AI-generated artworks
book_use: Chapter 14: participants were not consistently able to distinguish human from AI-generated images, while work believed to be AI-generated was evaluated less favorably; supports source-belief effects without treating human origin as a quality guarantee.

author_or_institution: Ariel Shank et al.
title: Perceptions of AI engaging in human expression
book_use: Chapter 14: human-versus-AI source beliefs and framing affected judgments differently across expressive tasks; use as counterevidence against a universal human-label premium.

author_or_institution: Alex B. Haynes et al.
title: A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population
book_use: Chapter 15: introduction of a 19-item checklist across eight hospitals was associated with lower observed complications and inpatient deaths; use as a concrete case of structured protective friction, not proof that all checklists work.

author_or_institution: David R. Urbach et al.
title: Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada
book_use: Chapter 15 counterevidence: mandatory checklist implementation in Ontario did not reproduce the dramatic outcome improvements of the original pilot; supports the distinction between functioning safety practice and compliance theater.

author_or_institution: Laura Freeman; Feras Batarseh; D. Richard Kuhn; M. S. Raunak; Raghu N. Kacker
title: The Path to Consensus on Artificial Intelligence Assurance
book_use: Chapter 15: AI assurance requires evidence across performance, data quality, security, explainability, and related dimensions; supports deliberate verification costs before consequential deployment.

author_or_institution: Michael I. Norton; Daniel Mochon; Dan Ariely
title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love
book_use: Chapter 16: successful self-assembly increased creators' valuation of their products, with important boundary conditions; supports a bounded effort/ownership mechanism, not a universal law that harder work is better.

author_or_institution: Justin Kruger; Derrick Wirtz; Leaf Van Boven; T. William Altermatt
title: The effort heuristic
book_use: Chapter 16: original experiments found perceived production effort could raise judgments of quality and value, especially under ambiguity; pair with the 2023 replication rather than treating the effect as settled or universal.

author_or_institution: Ignazio Ziano; Siu Kit Yeung; Cheong Shing Lee; Jiaxin Shi; Gilad Feldman
title: The Effort Heuristic Revisited: Mixed Results for Replications of Kruger et al. (2004)'s Experiments 1 and 2
book_use: Chapter 16 counterevidence: replications produced mixed support, including inconsistent monetary-value effects; use to bound claims about difficulty as a status or quality signal.

author_or_institution: Aparna A. Labroo; Sara Kim
title: The Instrumentality Heuristic: Why Metacognitive Difficulty Is Desirable During Goal Pursuit
book_use: Chapter 16: under some goal-pursuit conditions, experienced difficulty can increase perceived instrumentality; supports context-dependent valuation of effort rather than objective superiority of difficult means.

author_or_institution: International Energy Agency
title: Energy and AI — Executive summary
book_use: Chapters 17-18: data centres used about 415 TWh or 1.5% of global electricity in 2024; base case projects about 945 TWh in 2030. AI is an important driver but data-centre demand is not synonymous with AI demand; local concentration matters.

author_or_institution: International Energy Agency
title: Energy and AI — Energy demand from AI
book_use: Chapters 17-18: explains servers, cooling and data-centre energy demand; emphasizes spatial concentration, infrastructure lead times, efficiency uncertainty, and a wide range of 2035 scenarios. Use to show physical bottlenecks beneath digital abundance.

author_or_institution: International Energy Agency
title: Key Questions on Energy and AI — Executive summary
book_use: Chapter 18: energy per AI task has fallen rapidly while data-centre electricity consumption still rose 17% in 2025 and AI-focused facilities grew faster; supports a bounded rebound mechanism, not a universal Jevons-paradox claim.

author_or_institution: International Energy Agency
title: Energy and AI — Energy supply for AI
book_use: Chapter 18: physical supply mix and grid buildout remain consequential; renewables meet much of projected additional demand while gas, coal and nuclear also contribute. Supports material-system complexity rather than a single-fuel narrative.

author_or_institution: Alexander Chernev; Ulf Böckenholt; Joseph Goodman
title: Choice overload: A conceptual review and meta-analysis
book_use: Chapter 19: meta-analysis of 99 observations involving 7,202 participants found choice overload depends materially on decision difficulty, set complexity, preference uncertainty, and decision goals. Use as a conditional mechanism for selection burden, not a universal claim that more options are harmful.

author_or_institution: Raja Parasuraman; Dietrich H. Manzey
title: Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration
book_use: Chapter 20: review found automation complacency under divided-attention conditions in both novice and expert users and found simple practice did not eliminate the problem. Use as an older human-factors mechanism, not a direct performance estimate for modern generative-AI agents.

author_or_institution: OECD
title: Generative AI and the SME Workforce
book_use: Chapter 21: representative survey of more than 5,000 SMEs in seven countries; 31% reported GenAI use, with legal, information-handling and skills barriers. Twice as many users reported increased as decreased need for highly skilled workers. Use as bounded evidence about complementary institutional capability.

author_or_institution: National Institute of Standards and Technology
title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
book_use: Chapter 21: cross-sector guidance for identifying, measuring, managing and governing generative-AI risks across the lifecycle; use as evidence that deployment creates process and accountability work, not as a claim that one governance model fits every institution.

author_or_institution: International Labour Organization
title: Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure
book_use: Chapter 22: one in four workers globally are in occupations with some GenAI exposure while 3.3% of global employment is in the highest exposure category; emphasizes transformation more than wholesale replacement and documents unequal exposure across countries and groups.

author_or_institution: OECD
title: Generative AI
book_use: Chapter 22: more than one-third of individuals across OECD countries used generative AI in 2025, with large age gaps and meaningful education and income gaps. Date the statistics and do not assume adoption gaps are permanent.

author_or_institution: OECD
title: Macroeconomic productivity gains from Artificial Intelligence in G7 economies
book_use: Chapter 22: projected productivity gains vary materially across G7 economies because sector mix, exposure and adoption assumptions differ; use as evidence that the size of the dividend is institutionally and economically heterogeneous, not as a forecast guarantee.

author_or_institution: Simone Grassini; Mika Koivisto
title: Understanding how personality traits, experiences, and attitudes shape negative bias toward AI-generated artworks
book_use: Chapter 23: participants could not consistently distinguish human from AI-generated images; selected AI images were liked more on average, while images believed to be AI-generated were evaluated less favorably. Separates source belief from artifact quality.

author_or_institution: Christoph Fuchs; Martin Schreier; Stijn M. J. Van Osselaer
title: The Handmade Effect: What's Love Got to Do with It?
book_use: Chapter 23: four studies found a context-dependent handmade premium partly mediated by perceived love or care, especially for gifts; use as a bounded analogue for human-origin premiums, not as a universal willingness-to-pay rule.

author_or_institution: Ashley V. Whillans; Aaron C. Weidman; Elizabeth W. Dunn
title: Valuing Time Over Money Is Associated With Greater Happiness
book_use: Chapter 24: across six studies, prioritizing time over money was associated with greater subjective well-being after several controls; use as an association and orientation result, not a universal prescription to sacrifice income.

author_or_institution: Marissa A. Sharif; Cassie Mogilner; Hal E. Hershfield
title: Having Too Little or Too Much Time Is Linked to Lower Subjective Well-Being
book_use: Chapter 24: large U.S. data sets and experiments found a nonlinear relationship between discretionary time and well-being; too little time is costly, but more free time is not infinitely beneficial, especially without purposeful use. Bounds the claim that the final scarcity is simply leisure quantity.
